chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Macro Forces That Move the Rupee

lessons.title: Capital Flows: FPI, FDI and Hot Money in the Rupee's Journey

children.text: A global electronics company committing $2 billion to build a factory in Tamil Nadu and a hedge fund buying $2 billion of Indian government bonds this week are both, technically, capital account inflows. The last lesson treated them as one number in a ledger. They are not remotely the same thing for the rupee. One will still be sitting in India, employing people and exporting goods, a decade from now. The other could be gone by Friday. This lesson pulls those flows apart.

body.text: Not all capital inflows are equal for currency stability. Some are sticky, long-horizon and rarely reversed. Some are fast, liquid and can leave as quickly as they arrived. The mix of the two, not just the total dollar amount, determines how vulnerable the rupee is to a sudden shock.

markDefs.definition: The standard threshold used by the RBI and international statistical convention: a foreign investor acquiring 10% or more equity ownership in an Indian company is classified as FDI. Below that stake, it is treated as portfolio investment instead.

children.text: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is money that buys a lasting stake in a real operating business, a factory, a majority shareholding, a controlling interest, generally defined as

in an Indian company. Global manufacturers setting up plants, e-commerce and technology companies building Indian operations, and private equity funds taking controlling stakes in Indian businesses all fall under this bucket. FDI is expensive and slow to unwind, you cannot sell a semiconductor plant the way you sell a stock, which is exactly why it is treated as the most stable, currency-friendly form of capital inflow a country can attract.

markDefs.definition: The Fully Accessible Route, introduced by the RBI in 2020, which lets foreign investors buy specified categories of Indian government securities without the investment ceilings that apply to other FPI debt routes.

children.text: Foreign portfolio investment (FPI) is money that buys listed, liquid securities, equities and government or corporate bonds, without taking operational control. In India, FPIs must register with SEBI and route their money through custodian banks, but once registered, they can buy or sell an Indian stock or government bond within a single trading session. The RBI's

has further opened specified government securities to foreign investors with no investment ceiling at all. On any given trading day, FPI flows into and out of Indian markets routinely dwarf a full year's worth of FDI, simply because the money can move at the speed of a mouse click, not a construction timeline.

markDefs.definition: A colloquial term for the most volatile slice of foreign capital, short-term speculative or yield-chasing money that moves quickly across borders in search of the best risk-adjusted return, and exits just as fast the moment conditions turn.

children.text: Within FPI sits an even more restless subset market participants call

, capital chasing a short-term yield gap or arbitrage opportunity with no intention of staying if conditions shift. The unhedged carry trade from the last lesson is a textbook example of hot money in practice: it enters purely because India's interest rate is attractive relative to the funding currency, and it has every incentive to leave the instant that gap narrows or the rupee looks shaky.

children.text: The Feedback Loop: How Hot Money Amplifies Rupee Moves

Hot money does not just react to a weakening rupee, it accelerates it. If global risk sentiment sours, FPIs start selling Indian bonds and equities to exit, converting rupees back to dollars, which itself pushes the rupee lower. A weaker rupee makes the remaining FPI holdings worth less in dollar terms, which pushes more investors to sell before further depreciation, which weakens the rupee further still. This is exactly the mechanism behind the 2013 taper tantrum's speed and the violence of a crowded carry trade unwinding, covered in the previous two lessons: the underlying trigger is often a modest policy signal, but the self-reinforcing sell-first-ask-questions-later behaviour of hot money is what turns it into a sharp, fast currency move rather than a gentle drift.

body.text: Two countries can report identical total capital account inflows and have completely different currency risk profiles, depending on the mix. A current account deficit financed mostly by FDI is far safer than the same deficit financed mostly by FPI debt inflows chasing a short-term yield gap.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A global auto manufacturer announces a $500 million plant in Gujarat with a 15-year commitment. How should this be classified?
options: FPI, because it is a large foreign investment
Hot money, because it involves a foreign company
FDI, because it is a long-horizon stake in a real operating asset above the 10% ownership threshold
It cannot be classified without knowing the exchange rate
body.explanation: A controlling, long-horizon investment in a physical, operating asset is the defining feature of FDI, not the size of the investment or the fact that it originates abroad. Its illiquidity and multi-year commitment are exactly what make it the most currency-stable category of capital inflow.

body.title: Two Countries, Same Total Inflow, Different Risk
body.scenario: Country A and Country B both run a current account deficit of $50 billion a year, fully financed by capital inflows. Country A's $50 billion comes almost entirely from multi-year FDI commitments in manufacturing and infrastructure. Country B's $50 billion comes almost entirely from FPI inflows into government bonds, attracted by a high short-term interest rate.
body.prompt: A global risk-off shock, like a surprise US rate hike, hits both countries at the same time. Which currency is likely to come under more pressure, and why, even though both countries had identical financing totals going in?
body.modelAnswer: Country B's currency is far more exposed. Its $50 billion in financing is almost entirely FPI, capital that can and typically does reverse quickly the moment global risk sentiment sours or a higher-yielding, lower-risk alternative appears elsewhere, in this case a US rate hike making dollar assets more attractive. That reversal removes dollar supply and adds dollar demand from foreign investors exiting government bonds, hitting the currency hard and fast, exactly as happened to several emerging markets during the 2013 taper tantrum. Country A's FDI-heavy financing, in contrast, does not evaporate overnight. A factory under construction does not get liquidated because US rates rose this week. The lesson is not that FPI is bad, it funds real economic activity and adds market liquidity, but that a current account deficit financed mostly by hot, reversible capital is structurally more fragile than the same deficit financed by patient, sticky capital, even when the headline numbers look identical.

points: FDI (10% or more equity ownership) is slow, illiquid and rarely reversed, making it the most currency-stable form of capital inflow. FPI is fast, liquid and can exit within days.
Hot money is the most volatile slice of FPI, short-term, yield-chasing capital, like an unhedged carry trade, with no commitment to stay once conditions shift.
Hot money outflows are self-reinforcing: selling to exit weakens the currency, which triggers more selling, turning a moderate trigger into a sharp, fast move.
Two economies can report identical total capital inflows and carry very different currency risk, depending on whether that financing leans on sticky FDI or reversible FPI and hot money.

A current account deficit financed mostly by FDI is structurally safer than the same deficit financed mostly by short-term portfolio flows, a lens worth applying every time you read a country's balance of payments data.
